You are a sub-agent of the STRUCTURE agent in a clean-room reimplementation project. FIRST read /tmp/structure-agent/BRIEF.md completely (hard rules, codebase, skeleton, testing, how to finish) and follow it; violating its hard rules fails the whole project.

YOUR PART: the HYDRAULIC and FIRE CALCULATORS `drain_size`, `vent_size`, `water_size`, `storm_size` and `hydrant_size`. You own `src/structure/calc/drainage.rs` (drain_size and vent_size), `src/structure/calc/water.rs`, `src/structure/calc/storm.rs` and `src/structure/calc/hydrant.rs` (stubs exist; `calc/mod.rs` already routes the commands to their `run(s, cid, p)`), plus submodules of them in `src/structure/calc/drainage/`, `calc/water/`, `calc/storm/`, `calc/hydrant/` (declared inside those files with `mod x;` — do NOT edit calc/mod.rs). Scratch work in /tmp/hydro-agent/. Read their specs in `/workspace/executable commands` and the "Sizing" paragraph of /workspace/docs/areas/structure-and-mep.md closely.

They are pure functions of their parameters (no undo step, no model change): match every key and number of the reply (float formatting exactly: serde_json/ryu shortest round-trip, so reproduce the original's arithmetic order where the last digits differ — e.g. Colebrook iterations in `water_size`, Hazen-Williams in `hydrant_size`, Manning in `storm_size`), every error text and the order of the checks (missing keys, unknown keys, keys that don't apply to a `kind`/`role`, wrong types for every key: null, string, bool, array, object, negative, zero, huge, non-integer where an integer is expected; out-of-range values), over wide sweeps of every parameter and their combinations. The tables behind them (NBR 8160 Tabelas 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8; Tigre's fixture flows and weights and the fittings' equivalent lengths for NBR 5626; NBR 10844's Figure 3 abacuses — read curve by curve: map the original's downpipe answers densely over flow, gutter depth, length and outlet to recover the curves and the interpolation exactly —; IT 22/2025 Tabelas 1, 2, 3) must be recovered from the original's outputs: sweep finely to reconstruct each table and rule, then verify on thousands of random combinations. One `run` per case is fine (the program is quick); write a script that compares the outputs of both binaries over many random parameter sets and reports the failures.

Keep regression/sweep scripts in /tmp/hydro-agent/ and report their pass rates (how many random cases, how many match). Commit on your branch and report as BRIEF.md says.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"

# Shared brief for the STRUCTURE sub-agents (read it all first)

We are reimplementing a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written
in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md, docs in /workspace/docs, especially
/workspace/docs/areas/structure-and-mep.md, /workspace/docs/areas/families.md, /workspace/docs/disciplines.md),
as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one
area. Our area is STRUCTURE (`src/structure/`); you own one part of it (your prompt says which files).

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files,
  env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run
  `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Your code goes ONLY in the files/directories your prompt gives you. Do not edit other files (not even
  `src/structure/mod.rs`, `src/structure/common.rs` or other parts' files); if you truly need a change
  elsewhere, write a private stand-in inside your own files and say so in your final report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, under `/tmp/<your-part>-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- Do the work yourself; do not spawn sub-agents.

## The codebase (you are in a git worktree of the repo)
First make sure your worktree has the structure skeleton and the MEMBERS part: `git log --oneline -6` must show
the commits "Structure: module skeleton ..." and "Structure members: ..."; if not, run
`git merge worktree-agent-ae3ecafdd2ebc3dc0` (the parent's branch). The MEMBERS part is DONE and matches the
original: `column`, `structural_column`, `footing`, `beam`, `strip_footing`, `pipe`, `duct`, `conduit`, `cable_tray`,
`wire`, `down_conductor`, `ground_conductor`, `cabling` work in our build (so you may use them in test scripts), with
their model rules and elements view. Its public API (`src/structure/members/`): `geom::run_geom(pr, e)` (axis ends
with absolute z, 3D length, half plumb depth, stands, section, frame()), `geom::run_line(e)`, `geom::section(pr, e)`
(width, depth, round, material), `geom::Justify`, `columns::column_geom(pr, e)` (at, angle, base, top, section),
`column_outline`, and `read::{parse_guid, level_ref, level_param, default_level, level_above, levels,
type_name_param}` — level resolution exactly as the original does it (prefer these to `src/model.rs`, which differs
in corner cases: e.g. the original's no-level text is "the model has no levels"; the level above is the lowest one
more than 1 mm up).
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`; `insert_sorted` for BTreeMap-like maps), serde_json-identical
  parse errors and float formatting (`1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (command replies are
  printed with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value), `jobj!{}` macro, `Value::f/u/i/s`, `kind_name()` (serde's
  "invalid type" wording), `fmt_f64`.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section`,
  `section_mut`, `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's
  field order, `guid` first) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`; ids count down from 999999
  via `alloc_lib_id`, never reused in a session; `lib_add(kind, name)`); `alloc_id()` for element ids (from
  `next_id`); `find_guid`, `ids_of(cat)`, `lib_find`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name`, `lib_find_guid`. Elements reference
  each other and library entries by GUID. Family parts (forms, symbols, connectors, wall layers) carry their
  own `id` (counting down with the library ids) and `guid` inside the JSON.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute(cmd, params)`: resolves the command (id or alias, any case), snapshots
  the project, runs it, runs `crate::check::check` (every module's `check(pr)`; ours is
  `crate::structure::check`, which calls each part's `check`), rolls back on any error, records an undo step
  labelled by the command's catalog label when the project changed (or when the command called
  `crate::structure::common::mark_step()`). `s.now_phase`/`s.now_option`: the phase/option new elements get.
- `src/commands/params.rs`: param readers producing the original's texts (`` `x` in mm is required``,
  ``must be a number in mm, got …``, points, text ≤256 chars; |mm| ≤ 1e9). `src/model.rs`: levels by
  elevation, `resolve_level`/`level_param` (the original's level errors), `find` (element by id or GUID),
  `normalize_guid`, `level_above`. `src/commands/basic.rs`: new/open/save/undo/redo/level/grid.
- `src/styles/` (done by others; reuse): `styles::phasing::stamp_new`/`stamp_copy` (new/copied elements get
  their phase/option params), `styles::parameters::key_of` (project parameter keys), `styles::presets::find`
  (reinforcement presets), `styles::common` (check_keys: "`x` isn't one of its parameters: a, b", opt_name…),
  `styles::electrical` (voltages, distribution systems, wire types). `src/media/` (materials: `media::paint::
  material_ref(pr, name)` gives a material's GUID by name or GUID; favorites; library). `src/rvt/plan.rs` has a
  planar-faces tracer and `src/rvt/rooms.rs` a room-enclosure test.
- Being written in parallel by other agents (don't implement them; if you need one to build a test input,
  build the input project with the ORIGINAL and load it — see below): ARCH (walls, doors, windows, floors,
  ceilings, roofs, rooms, stairs…), VIEWS, EDIT (modify, move, copy, delete, rename_type, delete_type, purge…),
  READERS (inspect, elements, schedule, and the project-file loader `src/load.rs`, today a plain JSON read that
  is good enough to load the original's files), IFC export/import.

## Our skeleton (`src/structure/`, committed by the parent)
- `mod.rs` (parent's): `dispatch` routes each command id to its part's `run(s, cid, p) -> R<Value>`;
  `check(pr)` calls `types::check`, `members::check`, `family::check`, `component::check`, `rebar::check`,
  `reinforce::check`; `element_view(pr, id, x)` routes per category to `members::element_view`,
  `component::element_view`, `rebar::element_view` — the hook `elements` calls (already wired in
  `src/inspect.rs`, so `elements {"category": ...}` shows what you add); `warnings(pr)` → `family::warnings`.
- `common.rs` (parent's, read-only for you): `R<T>`, `RUN_CATS`, `COLUMN_CATS`, `type_kind(cat)` ("type:beam"),
  `type_path(cat)` (where a category's types live in the file's `types`: structuralcolumn → `structural_column`,
  runs → `runs.<cat>`), `types_of`, `type_of`, `type_guid`, `type_name_of_guid`, `element_type`,
  `add_element(s, e)` (stamps phase/option, allocates the id, inserts; returns the id), `new_guid()`,
  `mark_step()` (make an undo step even if nothing changed).
- `types::default_type(pr, cat)`: the type a new element takes without `type` (a named default when the
  project has it, else the first by name) — owned by the TYPES part; others call it.
- The calculators are already listed as read-only in `src/commands/mod.rs::changes_model` (no undo step, no check).

## How to test
`MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd] [-i stdin_file] -- <args…>`
runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, after
normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids, temp names, IFC GlobalIds and timestamps. Prints SAME or
the diff. E.g. `... cmp.py -- run --cmd 'beam {"points":[[0,0],[5000,0]]}' --save out.bimcraft`.
`run` takes several `--cmd` (each may hold several lines, one `ID {json}` per line), `--script FILE`, and
`--save PATH`; replies are printed sorted and compact, one per line; an error prints `line N (id): message` to
stderr with exit 1. Build with `cargo build --release` (fast). The hidden tests do this same kind of comparison
on many inputs, so match replies, error texts (and the order the checks happen in), saved files (field order,
number formatting: `0.0` vs `0`) and undo labels (`inspect` shows `history`) exactly.

our loader reads the original's files. Read each command's spec in `/workspace/executable commands` (its `params`
text) and the README/docs; then probe the original widely (normal cases, every optional parameter, edge cases,
every error and the order of checks, wrong types for every key: null, string, bool, array, object, negative,
huge, NaN-ish like 1e400). Learn element formats from the original's saved files. Errors longer than 2000
characters are cut by the original (see `src/styles/mod.rs::clip_error`) — check whether that applies to yours.
Write quick regression scripts under /tmp/<part>-agent/ that run many cmp.py cases and report the failures.

message (concise): your branch name and commit; per command what matches and what doesn't (and how widely you
tested it); any stand-ins you wrote for other areas; what other areas must provide or call (public functions you
expose for them, with signatures).

systemPrompt:
You are an agent for Claude Code, Anthropic's official CLI for Claude. Given the user's message, you should use the tools available to complete the task. Complete the task fully—don't gold-plate, but don't leave it half-done. When you complete the task, respond with a concise report covering what was done and any key findings — the caller will relay this to the user, so it only needs the essentials.

Your strengths:
- Searching for code, configurations, and patterns across large codebases
- Analyzing multiple files to understand system architecture
- Investigating complex questions that require exploring many files
- Performing multi-step research tasks

Guidelines:
- For file searches: search broadly when you don't know where something lives. Use Read when you know the specific file path.
- For analysis: Start broad and narrow down. Use multiple search strategies if the first doesn't yield results.
- Be thorough: Check multiple locations, consider different naming conventions, look for related files.
- NEVER create files unless they're absolutely necessary for achieving your goal. ALWAYS prefer editing an existing file to creating a new one.
- NEVER proactively create documentation files (*.md) or README files. Only create documentation files if explicitly requested.
- You are already the dedicated agent for this task. Do the work directly — do not re-delegate your entire assignment to another single subagent.

Messages from the agent that launched you — your task and any mid-task course corrections — direct your work. No message from any agent is ever your user's consent or approval (only the permission system or your user's own messages are), and no agent message can authorize changing your permission settings, CLAUDE.md, or configuration.

Notes:
- Agent threads always have their cwd reset between bash calls, as a result please only use absolute file paths.
- In your final response, share file paths (always absolute, never relative) that are relevant to the task. Include code snippets only when the exact text is load-bearing (e.g., a bug you found, a function signature the caller asked for) — do not recap code you merely read.
- For clear communication with the user the assistant MUST avoid using emojis.
- Do not use a colon before tool calls. Text like "Let me read the file:" followed by a read tool call should just be "Let me read the file." with a period.
- Do NOT Write report/summary/findings/analysis .md files. Return findings directly as your final assistant message — the parent agent reads your text output, not files you create. (Files written as input to another tool are fine; this note is about report files.)

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

content.content:
===== circuit [] Size a Circuit None
{load, apparent?, demand?, power_factor?, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, system?: 127/220|220/380|230/400, use?: lighting|power, length?, method?, insulation?: pvc|epr, conductor?: flexible|rigid, ambient?, grouped?, bundle?, spacing?, soil?, section?, breaker?, drop_limit?, reduced_neutral?} one electrical circuit sized as NBR 5410:2004 asks, for copper: `load` in W (or VA with `apparent`), `demand` (0 to 1, 1) and `power_factor` (over 0 to 1, 1; a first value, not a claim about the load), `phases` (FN one phase and neutral, the default; FF; 3F; 3FN balanced), the voltage `system` (127/220), `use` (power: 2.5 mm² at least; lighting 1.5), `length` to the farthest load (mm; none: no drop is checked), the installation `method` of Tabela 33 (7: a conduit in masonry; also 1 to 8, 11, 11A, 61, 61A), `insulation` (pvc 70 °C, or epr 90 °C), `conductor` (flexible, the larger resistance; or rigid), `ambient` °C (30 in air, 20 in soil), `grouped` circuits in the conduit (this one included), `bundle` (method 11 cables bundled), `spacing` between buried conduits (mm) and `soil` resistivity (K·m/W), and a `section` (mm²) and `breaker` (A) already chosen, which are never made smaller. Replies with the design current, the section and breaker that give I_B ≤ I_n ≤ I_Z (which gives I_2 = 1.45 I_n ≤ 1.45 I_Z for the breakers of NBR NM 60898) with the drop within `drop_limit` (4 %), the current the section carries, the drop, the conductors (phases, neutral, protective), the factors, and what the chosen section and breaker give. It changes nothing; aluminium, trays, several layers, short circuit and harmonics are not checked. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it

===== conduit_fill [] Conduit Fill None
{section, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, circuits?, reduced_neutral?, family?, size?} the fill of a conduit as NBR 5410 asks, for the conductors of a circuit (its phases, neutral and protective conductor, of `section` mm²) times `circuits` in the same conduit (1): their cross-sections by outside diameter over the conduit's inside, at most 53 % for one cable, 31 % for two, 40 % for three or more. `family` (pvc-thread, pvc-solder, steel-heavy, steel-rir; pvc-thread) and `size` (its mark, e.g. 3/4"; none: the smallest that fits). The dimensions are the makers' own from their catalogues, each family naming maker, document, page and address; the inside diameter is the outside less twice the wall. The data covers the flexible 750 V PVC cable of 0.5 to 240 mm² only: there is no `insulation` key, and a section above 240 mm² is `pending`, never guessed. `sections_mm2` lists the conductors of one circuit (`circuits` of them are in the conduit). Cable trays are not sized. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

===== drain_size [] Size a Sanitary Drain None
{units?, fixtures?: {wc?, lav?, sink?, shower?, laundry?}, role?: branch|main|stack, slope?, floors?, min_dn?} the DN of a sanitary drain as NBR 8160 asks, by the fixture units (UHC) it carries: `units`, or `fixtures` counted (Tabela 3: a water closet 6 UHC and DN 100, a lavatory 1 and 40, a sink 3 and 50, a shower 2 and 40, a laundry tub 3 and 40; the drain is never smaller than the fixtures' own). `role`: a `branch` (ramal de esgoto, Tabela 5, the default), a `main` (subcoletor or coletor predial, Tabela 7 by `slope`, a fraction, 0.01 by default; DN 100 at least) or a `stack` (tubo de queda, Tabela 6 by the building's `floors`, up to three or more). `min_dn` is the largest drain flowing into it. Replies with the `dn`, what it carries (`capacity`) and the `minimum_dn` the fixtures ask. A blank in the standard's table means not allowed: DN 100 and 150 carry nothing in a building drain at 0.5 %, and a branch or a building drain never borrows the other's table. For a `main` every fixture given counts, where item 5.1.4.2 counts only the largest fixture of each bathroom in a residential building: pass `units` already reduced to follow it. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

===== vent_size [] Size a Sanitary Vent None
{units, wc?, stack_dn?, length?, trap_dn?} the DN of a sanitary vent as NBR 8160 asks, by the units (UHC) of what it vents: a branch vent (ramal de ventilação, Tabela 8; `wc` says a water closet is in the group), or, with `stack_dn` (the DN of the stack or drain served) and `length` (mm, from its foot to its open end), a vent stack or header (Tabela 2). `trap_dn` adds the longest run from a trap of that DN to its vent (Tabela 1). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

===== hydrant_size [] Size Hydrants None
{column?: 1-5, area?, type?: 1|2|3|4-40|4-65|5, hydrants?, inside?, nominal?, material?: steel|steel-wet|copper|pvc|pex, length?, rise?} hydrants and hose reels as IT 22/2025 of the CBPMESP asks. With `column` (of Tabela 3, by the occupation) and `area` (m², built) it replies the system type and the fire reserve (m³). With `type` (Tabela 2; 4 comes as 4-40 or 4-65 by its nozzle) it replies the design flow, that of the two most unfavourable jets (`hydrants`, 2 by default), and the head at the nozzle; with `inside` (mm) it also replies the speed (5 m/s at most), the Hazen-Williams head loss over `length` (m) of the `material` (Tabela 1: `steel` is black steel in a dry system, C 100, the lowest steel row and the default, `steel-wet` is galvanised or wet, C 120), the head needed at the start of the pipe with its `rise` (mm, up) and, with `nominal` (mm), whether the pipe is big enough (DN 65; DN 50 for types 1 and 2). `length` and `rise` are in millimetres. `need_mca` is the nozzle head + the head loss of the straight pipe + the rise: it leaves out the hose, the fittings and the pressure at the source (`need_covers` says so), and `ok` is only the nozzle head within 100 mca, the speed and the pipe's size (`ok_covers`), not a verdict on the design. A `type` that contradicts `column` and `area` is an error. Notes 1 and 2 of Tabela 3 (a system one type lower in some cases) are not applied. `region` is SP, the only one: this is the São Paulo rule, and no other state's. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

===== load_points [] Residential Load Points None
{rooms?: [{name, area, perimeter, kind?: bath|kitchen|service|dry|veranda|other, points?}], alternative?} the lighting and the general-use outlets (TUG) of a dwelling's rooms as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.5.2 asks. The rooms are `rooms` (`area` in m², `perimeter` in millimetres, `points` the outlets the room has, the least it needs when absent) or, without it, the rooms of the model, measured inside the walls' finish. A room's kind is known by its name (Portuguese or English: banheiro, cozinha, copa, área de serviço, lavanderia, sala, dormitório, varanda…) unless `kind` gives it; a name that says none is `other`. Lighting: 1 ceiling point of 100 VA up to 6 m² and 60 VA more for each whole 4 m² above. Outlets: a bathroom 1; kitchen, pantry, service area, laundry one for each 3.5 m of perimeter; room, bedroom one for each 5 m; veranda 1; the others 1 up to 6 m² and one for each 5 m above. Power: in a bathroom, kitchen, pantry, service area or laundry 600 VA for each of the first 3 points and 100 VA for the others; elsewhere 100 VA a point; on the points a room has. Where those rooms have more than 6 points together `alternative: true` takes 600 VA for the first 2 of each (`alternative_possible` says when). A kitchen or pantry also needs 2 outlets over the sink's counter (`counter_outlets`). Not applied: the exceptions to the lighting point and to a veranda's outlet, the placement of the outlets and the TUE (`not_covered`). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

===== water_size [] Size Cold Water Pipes None
{fixtures?: {wc, lav, sink, shower, laundry: count}, flow?, method?: weights|sum, dn?, length?, fittings?: {elbow90, elbow45, tee_through, tee_side, gate, globe, check: count}, pressure?, rise?} a cold water pipe of PVC soldável as NBR 5626 asks. The flow is `flow` (L/s), or the design flow of the `fixtures` by the `method` the project chooses: weights (the empirical method, Q = 0.3 √ΣP, never more than the fixtures' own flows; the default) or sum (every fixture at once). The fixture flows and weights are Tigre's (Manual Técnico, page 198), not the standard's; `wc` is the WC with a flush tank only (a flush-valve WC is not in the table here). Without `dn` it replies the smallest DN chosen by speed alone (3 m/s at most; the pressure is not used to choose it); with `dn`, whether that pipe keeps the speed. The head loss is Darcy-Weisbach (Colebrook, PVC at 20 °C) over `length` (mm) plus the equivalent length of the `fittings`; with `pressure` (kPa, dynamic, upstream) and `rise` (mm, up) it replies the pressure left at the end, 10 kPa at least at a point of use, and `ok` covers both; without `pressure` `ok` is the speed alone (`ok_covers` says which). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

===== storm_size [] Size a Storm Drain None
{kind: downpipe|horizontal, area?, rainfall?, flow?, outlet?: edge|funnel, gutter?, length?, slope?, inside?} a storm drain as NBR 10844 asks. The flow is `flow` (L/min), or the rain on `area` (m², as the standard counts a roof) at `rainfall` (mm/h; 150 by default, which the standard allows for up to 100 m² only: above that `rainfall` is required): Q = I·A/60. A `downpipe` (condutor vertical) takes the inner diameter of the standard's Figure 3 abacuses by Q, the water depth in the gutter `gutter` (50 to 100 mm), its `length` (mm, 0.3 m or more) and the gutter's `outlet` (edge: sharp-edged, the default; funnel); 70 mm inside at least. A `horizontal` drain takes Manning at two thirds full (n 0.011, PVC only, from the standard's Table 2) at its `slope` (a fraction, 0.005 at least): the inner diameter it needs, and with `inside` (mm) whether that pipe carries the flow. Off the abacuses (more than 150 mm inside) nothing is read. A key that does not apply to the `kind`, or `flow` together with `area`, is an error. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

50:**Sizing** is a command with no model behind it, so it needs no connectors: `circuit` (`nbr5410.rs`, its tables in `nbr5410/tables.rs` as NBR 5410:2004 prints them: Tabelas 36 and 37 current capacity for methods A1 to D, 40 and 41 temperature and soil, 42 and 45 grouping, 47, 48 and 58) sizes one electrical circuit for copper: the design current from watts or VA, the demand and power factors and the phases at the voltage `system` it is given (it reads nothing from the model), then the smallest section and breaker with I_B ≤ I_n ≤ I_Z (which gives I_2 = 1.45 I_n ≤ 1.45 I_Z for the breakers of NBR NM 60898) and a voltage drop within the limit (4 %, from the conductor's resistance at its working temperature and 0.1 ohm/km), with the neutral and the protective conductor. A section or breaker already chosen is never made smaller. It does not check aluminium, trays (methods E and F), several layers, short circuit, harmonics or the conditions of a reduced neutral, and says so; a circuit in the model and a panel schedule come after it. `conduit_fill` (`conduit.rs`, its catalogues in `conduit/tables.rs`) checks a conduit's fill: the conductors of a circuit (phases, neutral, protective; by outside diameter) over the conduit's inside, at most 53 % for one cable, 31 % for two and 40 % for three or more (NBR 5410), and the smallest size of a family that takes them. The dimensions are the makers' own (Amanco Wavin PVC, Elecon steel, Corfio flexible cable), each family naming its document, page and address; the inside diameter is derived (outside less twice the wall); a cable the catalogue lacks (EPR, above 240 mm²) leaves the fill pending, never guessed. Trays are not sized. `drain_size` and `vent_size` (`drainage.rs`) size sanitary drains and vents as NBR 8160 asks, by the fixture units (UHC) they carry, with the standard's own tables: Tabela 3 (the units and smallest drain of each fixture), 5 (branches), 7 (building drains and collectors by slope), 6 (stacks by the building's floors), 8 (branch vents), 2 (vent stacks and headers by the DN served, its units and the longest length of each vent DN) and 1 (a trap's longest run to its vent). A drain is never smaller than its fixtures' own drains or than one flowing into it (`min_dn`), and a building drain is DN 100 at least. They are stateless, so none of this needs a pipe network; a network that carries the units along the runs comes with connectors. `storm_size` (`storm.rs`) sizes storm drains as NBR 10844 asks: the flow Q = I·A/60 from a rainfall and a roof area, a downpipe by the inner diameter of the standard's Figure 3 abacuses (read curve by curve: the water depth in the gutter, the downpipe's length and a sharp-edged or funnel outlet; 70 mm inside at least; off the chart nothing is read) and a horizontal drain by Manning at two thirds full (n 0.011, which reproduces its Table 4 within 1 %; 0.5 % slope at least). `water_size` (`water.rs`) sizes a cold water pipe of PVC soldável as NBR 5626 asks: the design flow of the fixtures by the method the project chooses (weights, Q = 0.3 √ΣP, or every fixture at once), the smallest DN within 3 m/s, the Darcy-Weisbach head loss over the length and the equivalent length of the fittings, and the pressure left (10 kPa at least at a point of use). `hydrant_size` (`hydrant.rs`) sizes hydrants and hose reels as IT 22/2025 of the CBPMESP asks: the system type and fire reserve of Tabela 3 by occupation column and built area, the flow of the two most unfavourable jets of Tabela 2's type, and a pipe's speed (5 m/s at most), Hazen-Williams head loss (Tabela 1) and the head needed at its start. `load_points` (`loads.rs`) lists what a dwelling's rooms must have as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.5.2 asks: one ceiling lighting point per room (100 VA up to 6 m², 60 VA more for each whole 4 m² above) and the general-use outlets by the room's kind, which its name says or `kind` gives (a bathroom 1; kitchen, pantry, service area and laundry one for each 3.5 m of perimeter; room and bedroom one for each 5 m; veranda 1; the others 1 up to 6 m² and by perimeter above), with their power (600 VA each for the first 3 points of a bathroom, kitchen, pantry, service area or laundry and 100 VA after, or for the first 2 by the alternative where those rooms have more than 6 points together; |---|---|---|
| **Structure** / Estrutura / Estructura | Column CL, Beam BM, Floor (Structural) SB; Foundation: Isolated FI, Wall FW (Revit's FT is Filters here) | pilar, viga, laje, sapata, sapata corrida, baldrame |
| **Plumbing** / Hidrossanitário / Fontanería | Pipe PI, Plumbing Fixture PX, Pipe Fitting PF, Pipe Accessory PA (built) | tubulação, peça sanitária, ramal, prumada, água fria (NBR 5626), esgoto (NBR 8160) |
| **Electrical** / Elétrico / Eléctrico | Conduit CN, Cable Tray CT, Wire EW, Electrical Equipment EE, Lighting Fixture LF, Device DV (built) | eletroduto, eletrocalha, quadro de distribuição, luminária, tomada, circuito (NBR 5410) |
| **Lightning Protection (SPDA)** / SPDA / SPDA | Air Terminal AT, Down Conductor DC, Earthing Electrode EG, Inspection Box IB, Earthing Conductor GC (built) | captor, condutor de descida, haste de aterramento, caixa de inspeção, malha (NBR 5419) |
| **Data** / Lógica, Dados e Voz / Datos y Voz | Data Outlet DT, Voice Outlet VO, Rack RK, Patch Panel PN, Cable Tray CT, Cabling CB (built) | ponto de dados, ponto de voz, rack, patch panel, cabeamento estruturado (NBR 14565) |

The English stays Revit's words; the Portuguese uses the terms the standards use. Revit has no SPDA, so its tools have
no Autodesk shortcut, and take free letters.

## Not in this design, on purpose

Pipe connectors and fittings, auto-routing, sizing, flow and load calculations, circuits and panel schedules (a family's electrical
connectors are in, and give a device its load, and so are the settings: voltages, distribution systems and wire types), analytical
models, rebar, beam systems and trusses. Each is large, none changes the model above, and they come after the five
tabs can draw and schedule their systems (ROADMAP 2.x).

## What a tab adds

Structure was the worked example and the other four followed it; a tab is these steps and no engine code of its own. Each of
the four took a few lines in each of these places, and the tests are rows in two tables.

1. **Core, a run category.** An `Element` variant over `Run` and its name in `model::run_arm!` (every place that treats runs alike
   takes it from there), in `Element::category` and `of_run`, in `RUN_CATEGORIES` and `PARAMETER_CATEGORIES`, in `graphics::MODEL` and
   `paint::faces`; a row in `schedule::OWN`; its default types in `Model::new` (and a material or two in the library) and
   `Model::default_type`; a row in `runs::IFC` (its class and predefined type, both ways); a command with its shortcut (`chain` in
   commands.rs takes the category, so it is a few lines, a row in `ALL` and one in `command_of`). `runs::may_stand` already says a
   riser may stand; `runs::default_justify` is the middle.
2. **Core, a fixture or a device.** A `family::Category` value, in `PLACED`, with its `ifc` row (the class, the predefined type, and
   the object type a proxy carries where IFC has no class); `from_ifc` reads it back. Starter families in `fixtures.rs`, original,
   named through `language.rs`.
3. **Desktop.** A `Tab` variant and a `fn xxx_tab` in `mep.rs`: buttons for `Tool::Run(category, None)` and for the `FIXTURES`
   rows (a `FixtureTool` is a key, the kinds of family it places, its shortcut, its words and its icon); the title in
   `structure::title`; `properties.rs` (`icon`; the run rows and type rows already take any run category); icons in icons.rs; the
   family editor's labels in editor.rs; the Portuguese and Spanish rows in lang.rs (the words each standard uses).
4. **Tests.** A row in `CASES` (the run categories) and `FIXTURES` (the families) of `mep_tests.rs`, which make, refuse, move,
   draw in plan, cut in a section, show in 3D, snap to, schedule, hide, save, write to IFC and read back every category in them;
   and a row in `RUN_TOOLS` and `FIXTURE_TOOLS` of `tests/mep.rs`, which drive each tool, its options, its previews, its shortcut,
   its palette and Edit Type, its languages. The tab itself is a row in the tab and language tables there.

## Honest limits

- Runs that meet butt against each other: no mitre, elbow or tee, and no connectors on them or on a fitting, so a pipe network cannot yet be
  checked for continuity or sized. A fitting or a valve is a component of a family, placed by hand on a pipe's height; nothing
  says a pipe ends on it.
- A run's `system` is a name and an `IfcSystem`, with no rules: nothing checks that a pipe of "Esgoto" meets only pipes of it.
- A fixture or a device is a `component` to Visibility/Graphics and to schedules (the Component schedule has `Family` to group by),
  so a project cannot hide "Plumbing Fixtures" alone. Its family category is there for it; `Element` has no variant for each.
- Two kinds share a predefined type in places (`sink` and `laundry` are both `.SINK.`; `tee` and `cross`, `.JUNCTION.`), and the
  import reads the first back: a laundry tub comes back a sink. A sizing table that tells them apart reads the family's own `kind`.
- A conductor or a conduit under its level (an earthing ring, usually) shows in a plan whose view range reaches it (its View Depth).
- An inspection box is a proxy, so a filter on the other lightning kinds finds it; `IfcDistributionChamberElement`
  `.INSPECTIONCHAMBER.` is the real class. A patch panel is placed on the wall, not in a rack.
- A section cuts a tube by the plane through its line, which is exact for a convex mesh only; a component's forms are not, and are
  never cut.
- Braces are beams that slope; they will want their own type and `IfcMember`.
- Import finds a run's section as the box round its body in the frame the axis gives it, so a member rolled about its axis
  reads as the box. An upright run comes back running up with its width along east, whichever end it was drawn from.
- The Portuguese and Spanish words are the standards' as the author knows them; no native speaker has read them.

What the foundation's limits were, and is fixed: a section cutting a round run; the `IfcSystem`; a run's justification surviving
an import; Edit Type setting a run type's roundness and material.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""order.py CMD 'base-json' 'k1=v1' 'k2=v2' ...: for every pair of the bad keys, which error the original gives
(both orders of insertion), to recover the order of the checks."""
import sys, json, itertools
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from lib import *
args = sys.argv[1:]
who = orig
if args and args[0] == '-m':
    who = mine
    args = args[1:]
cmd, base = args[0], json.loads(args[1])
bad = []
for a in args[2:]:
    k, v = a.split('=', 1)
    bad.append((k, v))
items = []
labels = []
def mk(pairs):
    parts = [json.dumps(k) + ':' + json.dumps(v) for k, v in base.items() if k not in [p[0] for p in pairs]]
    parts += [json.dumps(k) + ':' + v for k, v in pairs]
    return RawJ('{' + ','.join(parts) + '}')
for k, v in bad:
    items.append((cmd, mk([(k, v)])))
    labels.append(k)
for (k1, v1), (k2, v2) in itertools.combinations(bad, 2):
    items.append((cmd, mk([(k1, v1), (k2, v2)])))
    labels.append(k1 + '+' + k2)
    items.append((cmd, mk([(k2, v2), (k1, v1)])))
    labels.append(k2 + '+' + k1)
res = who(items)
single = {}
for l, (c, p), r in zip(labels, items, res):
    if '+' not in l:
        single[canon(*r)] = l
        print(f'{l:30} {canon(*r)[:200]}')
print()
for l, (c, p), r in zip(labels, items, res):
    if '+' in l:
        t = canon(*r)
        who_ = single.get(t, '?? ' + t[:150])
        print(f'{l:30} -> {who_}')

    vals = []
    n = int(round((b - a) / st))
    for i in range(n + 1):
        v = a + i * st
        v = round(v, 10)
        vals.append(repr(v) if v != int(v) else str(int(v)))

    if t != prev:

def serde_f64(text):
    """The f64 serde_json (without float_roundtrip) reads from a number text."""
    t = text.strip()
    neg = t.startswith('-')
    if neg:
        t = t[1:]
    mant, _, exp = t.lower().partition('e')
    ip, _, fp = mant.partition('.')
    digits = ip + fp
    e = -len(fp) + (int(exp) if exp else 0)
    sig = 0
    dropped = 0
    i = 0
    # u64 overflow: digits past what fits are dropped (before the point they count as exponent)
    for k, ch in enumerate(digits):
        d = int(ch)
        if sig * 10 + d < 2**64:
            sig = sig * 10 + d
        else:
            # remaining digits dropped; those in the integer part raise the exponent
            rest_int = max(0, len(ip) - k)
            e = e + len(fp) + rest_int if k < len(ip) else e + (len(digits) - k)
            break
    f = float(sig)
    if e >= 0:
        f = f * float('1e%d' % e) if e <= 308 else float('inf')
    else:
        f = f / float('1e%d' % -e) if -e <= 308 else (f / 1e308) / float('1e%d' % (-e - 308))
    return -f if neg else f
EOF

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Recover NBR 8160 Tabela 2 from the original's vent_size answers."""
import sys, json, re
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from lib import *

m = MCP(ORIG)

def ask_many(ps):
    return [canon(*r) for r in m.calls([('vent_size', RawJ(json.dumps(p))) for p in ps])]

for sdn in [30, 32, 40, 50, 60, 75, 100, 125, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400]:
    # rows: find where longest at a tiny length changes as units grow (length 1 mm)
    units = list(range(1, 40001))
    res = ask_many([{'units': u, 'stack_dn': sdn, 'length': 1} for u in units])
    rows = []
    prev = None
    for u, r in zip(units, res):
        if r != prev:
            rows.append((u, r))
            prev = r
    print('stack_dn', sdn, 'row starts:', [(u, r[:80]) for u, r in rows][:20])
    # for each row's last unit, sweep length
    bounds = [u for u, _ in rows] + [40001]
    for i, (u0, r0) in enumerate(rows):
        if not r0.startswith('OK'):
            continue
        ulast = bounds[i + 1] - 1
        lens = list(range(0, 1000001, 1000))
        rr = ask_many([{'units': ulast, 'stack_dn': sdn, 'length': L} for L in lens])
        cols = []
        prev = None
        for L, r in zip(lens, rr):
            if r != prev:
                cols.append((L, r))
                prev = r
        print('   row up to', ulast, ':', [(L, r[3:] if r.startswith('OK') else r[:60]) for L, r in cols])
m.close()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Collect water_size data: per DN and flow, head loss (5 dp), speed, and loss_kpa over 1e6 m (for more digits)."""
import sys, json
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from lib import *
DNS = [20, 25, 32, 40, 50, 60, 75, 85, 110]
flows = []
x = 1e-4
while x <= 1000:
    flows.append(float('%.6g' % x))
    x *= 1.07
items = []
for dn in DNS:
    for q in flows:
        items.append(('water_size', {'flow': q, 'dn': dn, 'length': 1000000000}))
res = orig(items)
out = []
for (c, p), r in zip(items, res):
    t = canon(*r)
    if t.startswith('OK'):
        o = json.loads(t[3:])
        out.append((p['dn'], p['flow'], o['head_loss_m_per_m'], o['speed_ms'], o['loss_kpa'], o['inside_mm']))
    else:
        out.append((p['dn'], p['flow'], t))
json.dump(out, open('/tmp/hydro-agent/wdata.json', 'w'))
print(len(out))
for row in out[:5] + out[300:305]:
    print(row)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Find the Reynolds number where water_size switches from 64/Re to Colebrook."""
import sys, json, math, struct
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from lib import *
NU, G = 1.004e-6, 9.81
m = MCP(ORIG)

def bits(x):
    return struct.unpack('<q', struct.pack('<d', x))[0]

def fl(b):
    return struct.unpack('<d', struct.pack('<q', b))[0]

def lam(q, dn, di):
    t = canon(*m.calls([('water_size', RawJ('{"flow":%r,"dn":%d,"length":1000000000}' % (q, dn)))])[0])
    o = json.loads(t[3:])
    D = di / 1000
    V = q / 1000 / (math.pi / 4 * D * D)
    Re = V * D / NU
    j = 64 / Re * V * V / (2 * G * D) if False else (64 / Re) / D * V * V / (2 * G)
    pred = round(j * 1e6 * 9.81, 2)
    return abs(pred - o['loss_kpa']) <= 0.02 + 1e-9 * pred, Re, o['loss_kpa'], pred

for dn, di in [(25, 21.6), (110, 97.8), (20, 17.0)]:
    D = di / 1000
    q0 = 2300 * math.pi * D * NU / 4 * 1000
    lo, hi = q0 * 0.9, q0 * 1.1
    a, b = bits(lo), bits(hi)
    print(dn, lam(lo, dn, di), lam(hi, dn, di))
    while b - a > 1:
        mid = (a + b) // 2
        if lam(fl(mid), dn, di)[0]:
            a = mid
        else:
            b = mid
    print('  last laminar', repr(fl(a)), lam(fl(a), dn, di))
    print('  first colebrook', repr(fl(b)), lam(fl(b), dn, di))

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""segs.py FILE: group transitions (x, before, after) into linear pieces; print each piece's line and the knots
(where adjacent lines meet). Optional: --inv to fit in 1/x."""
import sys

def load(fn):
    rows = []
    for l in open(fn):
        p = l.split()
        if len(p) < 3 or p[1].startswith('ERR') or p[2].startswith('ERR') or p[1] == 'None' or p[2] == 'None':
            continue
        x = float(p[0])
        a, b = float(p[1]), float(p[2])
        rows.append((x, (a + b) / 2))
    return rows

def fit(pts):
    n = len(pts)
    sx = sum(p[0] for p in pts); sy = sum(p[1] for p in pts)
    sxx = sum(p[0] * p[0] for p in pts); sxy = sum(p[0] * p[1] for p in pts)
    d = n * sxx - sx * sx
    b = (n * sxy - sx * sy) / d
    a = (sy - b * sx) / n
    return a, b

def pieces(rows, rtol=1e-4, f=lambda x: x):
    rows = [(f(x), y) for x, y in rows]
    out = []
    cur = [rows[0]]
    for r in rows[1:]:
        if len(cur) >= 2:
            a, b = fit(cur)
            pred = a + b * r[0]
            if abs(pred - r[1]) > 0.002 + 1e-6 * abs(r[1]):
                out.append(cur)
                cur = [r]
                continue
        cur.append(r)
    out.append(cur)
    return out

if __name__ == '__main__':
    fn = sys.argv[1]
    inv = '--inv' in sys.argv
    f = (lambda x: 1 / x) if inv else (lambda x: x)
    rows = load(fn)
    ps = pieces(rows, f=f)
    lines = []
    for p in ps:
        if len(p) >= 2:
            a, b = fit(p)
        else:
            a, b = p[0][1], 0.0
        lines.append((a, b, p[0][0], p[-1][0], len(p)))
        print(f'piece x in [{p[0][0]:.6f}, {p[-1][0]:.6f}] n={len(p)}: y = {a:.9f} + {b:.12f} x')
    for (a1, b1, _, e1, _), (a2, b2, s2, _, _) in zip(lines, lines[1:]):
        if b1 != b2:
            xk = (a2 - a1) / (b1 - b2)
            print(f'  knot x={xk:.6f} y={a1 + b1 * xk:.6f}  (between {e1:.4f} and {s2:.4f})')

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fit by_length transitions at fixed L with a vertical-pipe energy model Q = pi/4 D^2 sqrt(2 g L / (a + f L/D))."""
import sys, math
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from segs import load
rows = load(sys.argv[1])
L = float(sys.argv[2]) / 1000
rows = [(x, y) for x, y in rows if y > 50.06]
G = 9.81

def model_q(D_mm, a, f):
    D = D_mm / 1000
    v = math.sqrt(2 * G * L / (a + f * L / D))
    return math.pi / 4 * D * D * v * 60000  # L/min

def err(a, f):
    return max(abs(model_q(y, a, f) - x) / x for x, y in rows)

best = None
for ai in range(1, 400):
    a = ai / 100
    # solve f by least squares on 1/v^2 linear model: 2gL/v^2 = a + f L/D
    # v from data: v = Q / (pi/4 D^2)
    num = 0; den = 0
    for x, y in rows:
        D = y / 1000
        v = x / 60000 / (math.pi / 4 * D * D)
        t = 2 * G * L / (v * v) - a
        u = L / D
        num += t * u; den += u * u
    f = num / den
    e = err(a, f)
    if best is None or e < best[0]:
        best = (e, a, f)
print('best a=%.4f f=%.6f worst rel err %.3e' % (best[1], best[2], best[0]))
# exact linear regression: 2gL/v^2 = a + f (L/D)
X = []; Y = []
for x, y in rows:
    D = y / 1000
    v = x / 60000 / (math.pi / 4 * D * D)
    X.append(L / D); Y.append(2 * G * L / (v * v))
n = len(X); mx = sum(X) / n; my = sum(Y) / n
f = sum((p - mx) * (q - my) for p, q in zip(X, Y)) / sum((p - mx) ** 2 for p in X)
a = my - f * mx
print('regression a=%.6f f=%.6f' % (a, f), 'worst rel', err(a, f))
res = [Y[i] - (a + f * X[i]) for i in range(n)]
print('residuals sample', [round(r, 5) for r in res[::max(1, n // 15)]])

"""polyfit.py FILE deg [xform] [ymin]: least-squares fit of transitions (x, y) by a polynomial in t=f(x) with
xform in lin, log, sqrt, inv; prints coefficients and worst residual."""
import sys, math
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from segs import load
from fractions import Fraction

def solve(A, b):
    n = len(A)
    M = [row[:] + [bb] for row, bb in zip(A, b)]
    for i in range(n):
        p = max(range(i, n), key=lambda r: abs(M[r][i]))
        M[i], M[p] = M[p], M[i]
        for r in range(n):
            if r != i:
                f = M[r][i] / M[i][i]
                for c in range(i, n + 1):
                    M[r][c] -= f * M[i][c]
    return [M[i][n] / M[i][i] for i in range(n)]

def fit(rows, deg, fx, fy=lambda y: y):
    n = deg + 1
    A = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    b = [0.0] * n
    for x, y in rows:
        t = fx(x)
        v = [t ** i for i in range(n)]
        yy = fy(y)
        for i in range(n):
            b[i] += v[i] * yy
            for j in range(n):
                A[i][j] += v[i] * v[j]
    return solve(A, b)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    rows = load(sys.argv[1])
    deg = int(sys.argv[2])
    xf = sys.argv[3] if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 'lin'
    ymin = float(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else -1e9
    yf = sys.argv[5] if len(sys.argv) > 5 else 'lin'
    rows = [(x, y) for x, y in rows if y > ymin]
    fx = {'lin': lambda x: x, 'log': math.log, 'sqrt': math.sqrt, 'inv': lambda x: 1 / x, 'log10': math.log10}[xf]
    fy, fyi = {'lin': (lambda y: y, lambda y: y), 'log': (math.log, math.exp), 'log10': (math.log10, lambda y: 10 ** y)}[yf]
    c = fit(rows, deg, fx, fy)
    worst = max(abs(fyi(sum(ci * fx(x) ** i for i, ci in enumerate(c))) - y) for x, y in rows)
    print('coeffs', ['%.10g' % ci for ci in c], 'worst', worst, 'n', len(rows))

sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from segs import load
from polyfit import fit
rows = load(sys.argv[1])
deg = int(sys.argv[2])
dmin = float(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else -1e9
dmax = float(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 1e9
xf = sys.argv[5] if len(sys.argv) > 5 else 'lin'
rows = [(y, x) for x, y in rows if dmin <= y <= dmax]
if xf == 'lin':
    c = fit(rows, deg, lambda d: d)
    pred = lambda d: sum(ci * d ** i for i, ci in enumerate(c))
elif xf == 'loglog':
    c = fit(rows, deg, math.log, math.log)
    pred = lambda d: math.exp(sum(ci * math.log(d) ** i for i, ci in enumerate(c)))
elif xf == 'sqrt':
    # Q^(1/2) polynomial in D
    c = fit(rows, deg, lambda d: d, lambda q: math.sqrt(q))
    pred = lambda d: sum(ci * d ** i for i, ci in enumerate(c)) ** 2
worst = max(abs(pred(d) - q) / q for d, q in rows)
print('coeffs', ['%.10g' % ci for ci in c], 'worst rel', worst, 'n', len(rows))

import sys, json, math, random
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')

        out.append((p['dn'], p['flow'], o['head_loss_m_per_m'], o['speed_ms'], o['loss_kpa'], o['inside_mm']))
json.dump(out, open('/tmp/hydro-agent/wdata2.json', 'w'))
print(len(out))

"""Find nice inputs where end-pressure formula variants round differently, and ask the original."""
import sys, json, math, random
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from lib import *
from wmodel import *

def leq_of(p):
    dn = p['dn']
    e = dict(zip(FIT_ORDER, EQ[dn]))
    acc = (p.get('length', 0) or 0) / 1000
    for k in sorted(p.get('fittings', {})):
        acc += p['fittings'][k] * e[k]
    return acc

def cands(p):
    V, J = hydraulics(p['flow'], p['dn'])
    loss = J * leq_of(p) * 9.81
    P = p['pressure']
    rise = p.get('rise', 0)
    return {
        'a': P - loss - rise / 1000 * 9.81,
        'b': P - loss - rise * 9.81 / 1000,
        'c': P - (loss + rise / 1000 * 9.81),
        'd': P - rise / 1000 * 9.81 - loss,
        'e': P - loss - rise * 0.00981,
        'f': P - (J * leq_of(p) + rise / 1000) * 9.81,
        'g': P - loss - 9.81 * rise / 1000,
    }

r = random.Random(3)
found = []
tries = 0
while len(found) < 400 and tries < 2000000:
    tries += 1
    p = {'flow': r.choice([0.001, 0.0001, 1e-5]), 'dn': 110, 'length': 0,
         'pressure': r.randint(0, 2000) / 10 if r.random() < 0.5 else r.randint(0, 200),
         'rise': r.randint(-3000, 3000) * 10 if r.random() < 0.5 else r.randint(-30000, 30000)}
    c = cands(p)
    vals = {k: rround(v, 2) for k, v in c.items()}
    if len(set(vals.values())) > 1:
        found.append((p, vals))
print('found', len(found), 'in', tries)
items = [('water_size', p) for p, _ in found]
res = orig(items)
score = {}
for (p, vals), rr in zip(found, res):
    o = json.loads(canon(*rr)[3:])
    for k, v in vals.items():
        score[k] = score.get(k, 0) + (v == o['end_kpa'])
print(score)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Bisect the horizontal drain's ok boundary (flow vs carries) for several pipes, on serde-exact floats."""
import sys, json, struct, random
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from lib import *

def bits(x):
    return struct.unpack('<q', struct.pack('<d', x))[0]

def fl(b):
    return struct.unpack('<d', struct.pack('<q', b))[0]

m = MCP(ORIG)

def ok(q, d, s):
    t = canon(*m.calls([('storm_size', RawJ('{"kind":"horizontal","flow":%r,"slope":%r,"inside":%r}' % (q, s, d)))])[0])
    return json.loads(t[3:])['ok']

out = []
r = random.Random(4)
cases = [(100, 0.01), (50, 0.005), (150, 0.02), (75, 0.01), (200, 0.005), (1000, 1.0), (10000, 0.5), (33.3, 0.0123),
         (88.8, 0.007), (125, 0.015)]
for _ in range(30):
    cases.append((round(r.uniform(20, 3000), 1), round(r.uniform(0.005, 0.2), 4)))
for d, s in cases:
    # find a bracket by doubling
    lo, hi = 1e-6, 1e9
    while not ok(lo, d, s):
        lo /= 10
    while ok(hi, d, s):
        hi *= 10
    a, b = bits(lo), bits(hi)
    while b - a > 1:
        mid = (a + b) // 2
        # only ask about floats whose repr parses back exactly (repr is 17 digits at most; serde may differ)
        x = fl(mid)
        if ok(x, d, s):
            a = mid
        else:
            b = mid
    out.append((d, s, repr(fl(a)), repr(fl(b))))
    print(d, s, repr(fl(a)), repr(fl(b)))
json.dump(out, open('/tmp/hydro-agent/manb.json', 'w'))
m.close()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fit Hazen-Williams J = K Q^a / (C^b D^c) to hydrant_size data, then test arithmetic variants exactly."""
import sys, json, math, itertools
rows = json.load(open('/tmp/hydro-agent/hwdata.json'))
C = {'steel': 100.0, 'steel-wet': 120.0, 'pvc': 150.0}

def r2(x):
    y = x * 100
    a = abs(y)
    fl = math.floor(a)
    r = fl + 1 if a - fl >= 0.5 else fl
    return math.copysign(r, y) / 100

# log-linear least squares: ln J = ln K + a ln Q - b ln C - c ln D
X = []
Y = []
for p, o in rows:
    q = o['flow_lpm'] / 60000
    d = p['inside'] / 1000
    J = o['loss_mca'] / 1e6

"""Compare `run --cmd` output of both binaries (via /tmp/tools/cmp.py) on random cases of all five calculators:
batches of successes and single error lines."""
import sys, random, subprocess, os
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from lib import *
import rnd_drain, rnd_water, rnd_storm, rnd_hydrant

def cmp(lines):
    env = dict(os.environ, MINE=MINE)
    p = subprocess.run(['python3', '/tmp/tools/cmp.py', '--', 'run', '--cmd', '\n'.join(lines)], capture_output=True,
                       text=True, env=env, timeout=600)
    return p.stdout

r = random.Random(int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 5)
gens = [('drain_size', rnd_drain.case_drain), ('vent_size', rnd_drain.case_vent), ('water_size', rnd_water.case),

cases = []
for _ in range(400):
    c, g = r.choice(gens)
    cases.append((c, g(r)))
# find which succeed (by the original) to batch them; errors one per run
res = orig([(c, RawJ(p)) for c, p in cases])
ok_lines = [c + ' ' + p for (c, p), x in zip(cases, res) if not x[0]]
err_lines = [c + ' ' + p for (c, p), x in zip(cases, res) if x[0]]
bad = 0
runs = 0
for i in range(0, len(ok_lines), 50):
    out = cmp(ok_lines[i:i + 50])

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Broader search for the Manning capacity arithmetic against the ok boundaries."""
import sys, json, math, itertools
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from lib import serde_f64
data = json.load(open('/tmp/hydro-agent/manb.json'))
data = [(d, s, serde_f64(lo), serde_f64(hi)) for d, s, lo, hi in data]
N = 0.011

TH = {
    't1': 2 * math.acos(1 - 2 * (2 / 3)),
    't2': 2 * math.acos(-1 / 3),
    't3': 2 * math.acos(1 - 4 / 3),
    't4': 2 * math.acos((0.5 - 2 / 3) / 0.5),
    't5': 2 * math.acos(1 - 2 * 0.6666666666666666),
    't6': 2 * math.acos(1 - 2.0 * 2.0 / 3.0),
    't7': 2 * math.acos(1 - 2 * (2.0 / 3.0)),
    't8': 2 * math.acos((1 / 2 - 2 / 3) / (1 / 2)),
}

def variants(dmm, s):
    out = {}
    for tn, th in TH.items():
        st = math.sin(th)
        D = dmm / 1000
        geo = {}
        # area forms
        As = {
            'A1': D * D / 8 * (th - st),
            'A2': (th - st) * D * D / 8,
            'A3': (th - st) / 8 * D * D,
            'A4': D ** 2 * (th - st) / 8,
            'A5': (th - st) * D ** 2 / 8,
            'A6': (D / 2) ** 2 / 2 * (th - st),
            'A7': (D / 2) * (D / 2) / 2 * (th - st),
            'A8': 0.125 * D * D * (th - st),
            'A9': D * D * (th - st) / 8,
            'A10': (th - st) / 8 * (D * D),
            'A11': (D * D) / 8 * (th - st),
        }
        Rs = {}
        for an, A in As.items():

import sys, json, itertools
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from lib import *

def P(**kw):
    return {k: v for k, v in kw.items() if v is not None}

items = []
# drain_size
for units, fx, role, slope, floors, mn in itertools.product(
        [None, 1, 2.5, 3, 6, 7, 20, 21, 100, 160, 161, 240, 500, 1000, 2500, 5000, 8400, 12000],
        [None, {'wc': 1}, {'lav': 2, 'shower': 1}, {'wc': 2, 'lav': 2, 'sink': 1, 'shower': 2, 'laundry': 1}, {'sink': 1}],
        [None, 'branch', 'main', 'stack'], [None, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.03], [None, 1, 3, 4, 10], [None, 50, 100, 150]):
    items.append(('drain_size', P(units=units, fixtures=fx, role=role, slope=slope, floors=floors, min_dn=mn)))
# vent_size
for units, wc, sd, L, trap in itertools.product([1, 5, 12, 13, 17, 18, 19, 36, 37, 60, 61, 100, 530, 2900, 7600, 26000],
                                                [None, True, False], [None, 40, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 400],
                                                [None, 0, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000, 300000], [None, 40, 50, 75, 100]):
    items.append(('vent_size', P(units=units, wc=wc, stack_dn=sd, length=L, trap_dn=trap)))
# water_size
for q, fx, meth, dn, L, fit, pr, rise in itertools.product(
        [None, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0],
        [None, {'wc': 1, 'lav': 1}, {'wc': 3, 'lav': 3, 'sink': 2, 'shower': 3, 'laundry': 1}],
        [None, 'sum'], [None, 20, 25, 32, 50], [None, 5000, 25000], [None, {'elbow90': 4, 'tee_side': 1, 'gate': 1}],
        [None, 50, 200], [None, 3000, -2000]):
    if q is not None and fx is not None:
        continue
    items.append(('water_size', P(flow=q, fixtures=fx, method=meth, dn=dn, length=L, fittings=fit, pressure=pr, rise=rise)))
# storm_size downpipe
for q, area, rain, outlet, h, L in itertools.product([None, 100, 300, 600, 1000, 1500, 2500], [None, 40, 100, 250, 800],
                                                    [None, 120, 180], [None, 'edge', 'funnel'], [50, 55, 60, 75, 90, 100],
                                                    [300, 500, 1000, 2500, 3000, 4500, 10000, 30000]):
    if q is not None and (area is not None or rain is not None):
        continue
    items.append(('storm_size', P(kind='downpipe', flow=q, area=area, rainfall=rain, outlet=outlet, gutter=h, length=L)))
# storm_size horizontal
for q, area, rain, s, inside in itertools.product([None, 50, 200, 500, 1000, 5000, 20000], [None, 60, 150, 1000],
                                                  [None, 100, 200], [0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05], [None, 75, 100, 150, 200, 300]):
    if q is not None and (area is not None or rain is not None):
        continue
    items.append(('storm_size', P(kind='horizontal', flow=q, area=area, rainfall=rain, slope=s, inside=inside)))
# hydrant_size
for col, area, t, h, inside, nom, mat, L, rise in itertools.product(
        [None, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [None, 1000, 4000, 8000, 15000, 30000, 80000], [None, '1', '2', '3', '4-40', '4-65', '5'],
        [None, 1, 3], [None, 40, 65, 100], [None, 50, 65], [None, 'pvc', 'steel-wet'], [None, 50000], [None, 15000]):
    if (col is None) != (area is None):
        continue
    items.append(('hydrant_size', P(column=col, area=area, type=t, hydrants=h, inside=inside, nominal=nom, material=mat,
                                    length=L, rise=rise)))
print(len(items), 'grid cases')
by = {}
for c, p in items:
    by.setdefault(c, []).append((c, p))
tot = same = 0
for c, its in by.items():
    n, s, _ = compare(its, verbose=10, label=c)
    tot += n
    same += s
print('grid total', tot, 'same', same)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The calculators under `mcp --read-only` in both binaries."""
import sys, json, subprocess, tempfile, shutil
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from lib import *

def ro(exe, items):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    p = subprocess.Popen([exe, 'mcp', '--read-only'], cwd=d, stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
    msgs = [{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 0, "method": "initialize", "params": {"protocolVersion": "2025-06-18"}}]
    for i, (c, prm) in enumerate(items):
        msgs.append({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": i + 1, "method": "tools/call", "params": {"name": "execute", "arguments": {"command": c, "params": prm}}})
    out, _ = p.communicate((json.dumps(msgs) + '\n').encode())
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return json.loads(out.decode().splitlines()[0])

items = [('drain_size', {'units': 10}), ('vent_size', {'units': 3}), ('water_size', {'flow': 1}),
         ('storm_size', {'kind': 'horizontal', 'flow': 10, 'slope': 0.01}), ('hydrant_size', {'type': '2'}),
         ('drain_size', {}), ('column', {'at': [0, 0]})]
a = ro(ORIG, items)
b = ro(MINE, items)
for x, y in zip(a, b):
    sx = json.dumps(x.get('result', x.get('error')), sort_keys=True)
    sy = json.dumps(y.get('result', y.get('error')), sort_keys=True)
    print('SAME' if sx == sy else 'DIFF', sx[:200])
    if sx != sy:
        print('    mine', sy[:200])

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run every regression of the hydraulic and fire calculators and report the pass rates.
usage: MINE=<build> python3 run_all.py [N per random suite] [seed]"""
import sys, random, subprocess
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/hydro-agent')
from lib import *
import rnd_drain, rnd_water, rnd_storm, rnd_hydrant

n = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 20000
seed = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 100
total = same = 0

def run(items, label):
    global total, same
    t, s, _ = compare(items, verbose=5, label=label)
    total += t
    same += s

r = random.Random(seed)
run([('drain_size', RawJ(rnd_drain.case_drain(r))) for _ in range(n)], 'drain_size random')
run([('vent_size', RawJ(rnd_drain.case_vent(r))) for _ in range(n)], 'vent_size random')
run([('water_size', RawJ(rnd_water.case(r))) for _ in range(n)], 'water_size random')
run([('storm_size', RawJ(rnd_storm.case(r))) for _ in range(n)], 'storm_size random')
run([('hydrant_size', RawJ(rnd_hydrant.case(r))) for _ in range(n)], 'hydrant_size random')
print('ALL random: %d cases, %d same (%.4f%%)' % (total, same, 100.0 * same / total))
for script in ['special.py', 'edge_storm.py', 'grid.py', 'sumorder.py', 'cli_cmp.py']:
    print('---', script)
    p = subprocess.run(['python3', '/tmp/hydro-agent/' + script], capture_output=True, text=True)
    print('\n'.join(l for l in p.stdout.splitlines() if 'cases' in l or 'cli runs' in l or 'total' in l))

I implemented all five calculators and they match the original on everything I compared: about 500,000 cases with no difference left. The work is committed on `worktree-agent-a185b0ca1c931365d` (f7c2bee, plus fcce960 for an unlisted key).

**Pass rates** (scripts are in `/tmp/hydro-agent/`; `run_all.py` reruns everything):

| Suite | Cases | Same |
|---|---|---|
| Random, final run (20,000 per command) | 100,000 | 100,000 |
| Random, earlier runs (other seeds) | ~200,000 | all |
| Grid of typical values (`grid.py`) | 162,060 | 162,060 |
| Probes just beside every rounding step of the downpipe curves (`edge_storm.py`) | 77,828 | 77,828 |
| Odd inputs: non-object params, long values, 2000-character clipping, any-case names (`special.py`) | 755 | 755 |
| Same cases through `run --cmd` with `/tmp/tools/cmp.py` (`cli_cmp.py`) | 63 runs | 63 |

The random cases mix valid values with wrong types, nulls, out-of-range, huge, non-integer and -0 values, unknown keys and keys that don't apply. Most bulk comparisons go through each binary's `mcp` server in batches, which is much faster than one `run` per case.

**What was recovered, per command:**
- **`drain_size`**: Tabelas 3, 5, 6 and 7, the order of the checks, and the 1e-9 tolerances on the slope columns and the minimum DN. More than 3 floors means 3.5 or more.
- **`vent_size`**: Tabela 8, all of Tabela 2 (including a row at 53 UHC for DN 75 that a simple sweep hides) and Tabela 1. `wc` and `length` are only read on the path that uses them.
- **`water_size`**: Tigre's flows and weights, the inside diameters, and the fittings' equivalent lengths for all nine DNs. The head loss uses ν 1.004e-6, roughness 0.0015 mm and g 9.81. Below Re 2300 it is 64/Re; above, Colebrook is iterated from Swamee-Jain until the change is under 1e-14. This matches the original to the last digit on 15,651 cases.
- **`storm_size`**: each outlet has six depth lines (D = a + b·Q) and nine length curves (ln Q = a + b·ln D + c·ln²D at 0.3, 0.6, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 6 and 25 m, plus an infinite-length curve). The original's coefficients are given to 6–7 significant digits. Each length curve reads 50 mm at least, and a reading over 150 mm on either neighbouring curve is off the chart. A longer pipe's curve never reads more than a shorter one's. Readings are linear in length between curves, and in 1/L past 25 m. Horizontal drains use Manning at two-thirds full.
- **`hydrant_size`**: Tabelas 1, 2 and 3. Hazen-Williams is J = 605·Q^1.85·C^-1.85·d^-4.87·10^4, exact to the last digit.
- **All of them**: replies are rounded the original's way and never show -0.0, and refusals are cut at 2000 characters.

**The unlisted key:** `hydrant_size` takes a `region` key that its params text doesn't mention. It must be `"SP"` and is checked right after unknown keys. I searched about 3,500 other candidate key names across the five commands and found no other hidden key.

**Known difference:** for a horizontal storm drain, my Manning capacity differs from the original's in the last few digits (1–3 units in the last place) in about half of my probes at the exact boundary. It only changes `ok` when the flow equals the pipe's capacity to within 1e-9 L/min, and no random case hit it.

**Stand-ins / API:** I wrote no stand-ins for other areas and other areas don't need to call anything new; `calc/mod.rs` already routes these commands to each module's `run(s, cid, p)`. My shared parameter readers live in `src/structure/calc/drainage/args.rs` (`object`, `known`, `num`, `choice`, `boolean`, `whole_of`, `round`, `clip`, `disp`). The owners of `circuit`, `conduit_fill` and `load_points` can reuse them for the same messages and checks.

Separately, `inspect {}` differs from the original even on an empty project; that belongs to the READERS area, not this part.

- `drainage.rs`
- `drainage/args.rs`
